title: US black mass export restrictions could bolster domestic refiners
gist: The Trump administration invoked Section 101 of the Defense Production Act on 30 July 2026 to control exports of recoverable critical minerals, and BIS followed on 4 August with a temporary rule requiring US sellers of black mass and tungsten scrap to allocate 100% of monthly sales to US persons absent a license. Benchmark's read is that the captive feedstock should redirect volumes to US recyclers, with the open questions being whether it actually accelerates domestic refining buildout or simply gets circumvented. The piece is a short news item truncated by a subscriber paywall prompt, so the analysis stops at the framing question.

themes.theme: DPA Section 101 as a critical-minerals export lever

insights.claim: On 30 July the Trump administration issued a memorandum using Section 101 of the Defense Production Act to secure supply of recoverable Critical Minerals and Materials by controlling their exports, explicitly including black mass and used batteries in scope.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: The DPA is now being used as an export-control instrument for recycled battery feedstock, not just for domestic production incentives — widening the set of materials that can be captured onshore by executive action.

insights.claim: Scrap and recycled intermediates such as black mass and tungsten waste are being treated by US policy as strategic critical-mineral feedstock subject to export licensing, placing secondary supply on the same regulatory footing as primary mined material.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Recyclers and scrap traders with US-origin material face a policy regime previously reserved for mined critical minerals; export-dependent scrap business models need rerating.

themes.theme: The BIS temporary rule mechanics and timeline

insights.claim: On 4 August the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security issued a temporary rule restricting exports of black mass and tungsten scrap without a license, and is currently seeking public feedback on it.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A licensing requirement is already live in draft form — exporters cannot assume business-as-usual shipments past the implementation date.
insights.locator: issued a temporary rule to restrict exports of black mass and tungsten scrap

insights.claim: The BIS rule requires US persons selling black mass and tungsten waste and scrap to allocate 100 percent of monthly sales to US persons unless an adjustment or exception is obtained in advance from BIS.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A 100% domestic allocation mandate is effectively a hard export ban with a discretionary carve-out, which should compress US domestic black mass prices relative to export-parity levels while tightening ex-US feedstock.
insights.quote: U.S. persons engaged in the sale of black mass and tungsten waste and scrap must allocate 100 percent of monthly sales to U.S. persons, unless an adjustment or exception is obtained in advance from BIS.

insights.claim: The rule was published on 6 August with a 21-day feedback window, official implementation on 27 August and an expiration date of 17 September 2027, giving the restriction a defined roughly two-year life.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: 27 August is the hard date for feedstock flow changes and 17 September 2027 is the sunset to watch; the finite expiry limits how much permanent refining capex the policy alone can justify.
insights.quote: there are 21 days permitted for feedback before official implementation on 27 August with an expiration date of 17 September 2027

insights.claim: Benchmark's senior black mass pricing analyst expects an export ban on black mass to redirect feedstock toward US recyclers, implying a structural improvement in domestic utilisation rates for existing US recycling assets.
insights.speaker: Frederick Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Domestic recyclers and refiners with idle or underfed capacity are the direct beneficiaries; feedstock scarcity has been a key constraint on their economics.
insights.quote: A ban on the export of black mass should redirect feedstock towards US recyclers
insights.locator: said Frederick Bloomfield, a senior black mass pricing analyst

insights.claim: The decisive uncertainty is whether the export restriction actually accelerates buildout of US black mass refining capacity and stops critical mineral leakage, or whether the rules simply get circumvented — feedstock capture alone does not guarantee downstream refining investment.
insights.speaker: Frederick Bloomfield
insights.so_what: Track announced US black mass refining capacity additions and BIS exception grants after 27 August as the tell for whether this is a real reshoring catalyst or a paper restriction.
insights.quote: The key question is whether the policy will accelerate the buildout of US black mass refining capacity and mitigate critical mineral leakage, or whether these rules can be circumvented.

insights.claim: The framing of 'critical mineral leakage' implies the US currently exports recoverable battery-metal units embedded in black mass to overseas refiners rather than capturing them domestically, making the export rule a leakage-plugging measure rather than a supply-creating one.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Onshore refining capacity, not scrap collection, is the binding constraint — the investable gap is US hydrometallurgical black mass processing.
